content: Between 2018 and 2020, a budget of $150,000 was allocated for analyzing data on the use of bedaquiline in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) in South Africa. One member of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), Hoa Binh Nguyen, disclosed a conflict of interest. Nguyen was a team member of the V-QUIN trial and received a monthly payment of approximately $100 from the Woolcock Institute in Australia for this work. Consequently, Nguyen was recused from the meeting. Members of the External Review Group (ERG) who declared no conflicts of interest with the objectives of the guidelines included Anurag Bhargava, Marie Diaz, Anthony D. Harries, Nino Lomtadze, Lindiwe Mvusi, Ruslan Malyuta, Giovanni B. Migliori, Anastasia Samoilova, Alena Skrahina, Carrie Tudor, and Valentina Vilc. Other ERG members declared interests that were deemed not to conflict with WHO policies or the meeting's objectives. For example, Helen Ayles reported receiving in-kind support for her research group in the form of test kits for tuberculosis infection (TBI) diagnosis from BD Biosensor (valued at $5,000), Serum Institute of India (valued at $2,000), and Qiagen (valued at $2,000). She also disclosed support from a Stop TB Partnership TB Reach grant for scaling up tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) alongside TBI testing, amounting to $699,734. Gavin Churchyard reported research support from Sanofi to his employer, the Aurum Institute, in the form of donated rifapentine and isoniazid for the WHIP3TB trial, valued at approximately $350,000. He also participated in a Sanofi advisory board on rifapentine for TPT without receiving travel support or payment. Additionally, he disclosed a donation of rifapentine from Lupin Ltd for IMPAACT4TB studies, valued at $300,000, and an honorarium of $1,100 from Janssen Pharmaceuticals for participating in an advisory board on developing long-acting injectable formulations of bedaquiline. Amita Gupta reported receiving research grants to her university from the US National Institutes of Health, UNITAID, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the US Agency for International Development, and the Wyncote Foundation, with amounts unspecified. Raquel Duarte disclosed several grants, including the UNITE4TB project (2021–2028), the EUSAT-RCS project (2019–2024), and the UrbanTB project (2018–2022). She also works as a tuberculosis consultant for the Portuguese national and regional TB programs and is a member of the TB Disease Network Coordination Committee of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Evidence reviewers were responsible for data collection, summarization, and providing estimates for evidence summaries but did not participate in formulating policy recommendations. Stephanie Law and Harsimren Sidhu, evidence reviewers, declared no conflicts of interest with the guidelines' objectives. The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis prevention and treatment include detailed evidence summaries and recommendations. These guidelines address various aspects of tuberculosis prevention, including the prevalence of TB infection, the risk of progression to active TB disease, and the effectiveness of different preventive treatment regimens. The guidelines also evaluate the accuracy of diagnostic tools, such as WHO symptom screening and interferon-gamma release assays, in identifying individuals at risk of TB progression. The guidelines emphasize the importance of considering individual and contextual factors in TB prevention and treatment strategies. They also highlight the challenges of heterogeneity among studies, potential biases, and limitations in sample sizes, which may affect the reliability of evidence. For example, studies on household contacts of TB patients often show variability in TB incidence due to differences in background TB prevalence and study methodologies. The guidelines provide specific recommendations for preventive treatment regimens, such as the use of 3-month daily rifampicin plus isoniazid (3RH) for children and adolescents under 15 years of age, and 4-month daily rifampicin for individuals of all ages at risk of TB disease. They also explore the safety and efficacy of shorter regimens, such as 1-month daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, compared to longer regimens like 6 or 9 months of isoniazid monotherapy. In high TB incidence settings, the prevalence of TB infection and disease is often higher among household contacts of TB patients compared to the general population. However, the guidelines note that ascertainment bias is likely, as TB cases in the general population are typically detected passively, while cases among household contacts are actively identified. This may lead to overestimation of relative and absolute risks. The guidelines also address the cumulative prevalence of active TB among household contacts, irrespective of baseline TB infection status, and compare it to the general population. They highlight the need for further research to address gaps in evidence, particularly in high TB incidence countries.
